title: [3.x] `Physics` - Fix `wake_neighbours` behaviour (3D)

milestone.title: 3.x
milestone.description: Issues and pull requests slated for an undetermined Godot 3 release.

body:
Alternative to #124215, currently probably my preferred method.

Fixes a number of bugs in `Static` and `Kinematic` bodies.

Fixes #64890.

### `Bullet`
* fixes forward movement with `set_transform()` wakes bodies (now matches `GodotPhysics`)
* fixes previous location with `set_transform()` wakes bodies (now matches `GodotPhysics`)

### `Bullet` and `GodotPhysics`
Adds new `wake_neighbors()` command, which allows users to manually wake neighbors when removing bodies, or enabling / disabling `CollisionShapes`.

This allows users to correctly deal with the problem of removing e.g. a Platform,and having objects on the platform fall, instead of hanging in mid air.

### `Bullet` `wake_neighbours()` versus `GodotPhysics`
I considered 3 mechanisms for waking:
* The approach in #124215. This however went through _all pairs_ in the space for each object, so would scale badly.
* Waking all bodies in a linked island. Unfortunately `Bullet` aggressively removes sleeping objects from islands, so this wasn't going to work.
* AABB / sweep test.

I'm current using an AABB test as it should be fast. There are some situations where it won't be as efficient, for instance a long thin off axis object could potentially wake other objects unnecessarily. On the other hand it has to be _fast_ for small objects that are doing previous AABB checks on movement. In most cases the quick reject (as moved last tick) will prevent this, but not likely all cases.

## Manual versus Automatic
This PR requires the user to manually call a function in order to wake neighbors, whereas #124215 does this automatically. The trade-off here is that although the user has to make an explicit call (which is not obvious, and is a bit of gotcha), it avoids potential performance issues when unloading scenes (which would otherwise wake rigid bodies as each object is removed).

My current view is that automatic handling of wakeup is a laudable goal (hence making #124215 first). However, @jrouwe is correct that there are some situations where this currently _may_ have performance implications, especially streaming.

In 3.x the emphasis is on backward compatibility so that does lean me slightly towards preferring manual API call (at least to start with), because there should be no implications for existing games, and it is _opt-in_.

The other advantage is that if we _do_ roll out automatic wakeup PRs (e.g. #121748), we can make `wake_neighbor()` calls a NOOP in that particular situation, so there is no cost (and possibly emitting a warning that it is no longer required in that situation).

## Initial placement
Note that this PR doesn't attempt to deal with the general existing problem of physics inefficiency in initial placement, this probably needs its own investigation and PR. This is historical and due to bodies being initially added at the origin before being _placed_ in their start positions. This both stresses the broadphase unnecessarily, and also can potentially attempt to unnecessarily wakeup objects _at the origin_ due to the initial move.

Additionally we may want a special case here longterm, so as to be able to e.g. stream in parts of a world with RigidBodies sleeping, rather than being woken due to initial placement.

## Notes
* Provided as an alternative, we are still weighing up which approach to go with here.
* Uses the horrible US spelling of neighbours, as this is Godot convention. :grin: 
* We could if desired, keep the mechanism of auto-waking bodies when enabling / disabling collision shapes (I've omitted this for now, leaving the user to call `wake_neighbors()` manually).
* If the approach of auto calling it for previous AABBs on movement proves too expensive in a beta version, we could remove that and instruct the user to call `wake_neighbours` manually in the case of e.g. teleporting objects. _(athough note that would keep the difference in behaviour between godot physics and bullet here, as godot physics handles the previous AABB correctly.)_
* Same problem (collision shapes and removal) occurs in 4.x, so we can possibly use the same approach there.
